subject: Copywriting
subcategory: The Science of Storytelling in Ads
title: The Three-Act Structure
description: Learn The Three-Act Structure in one minute.

hook.text: Every Hollywood movie follows three acts: setup, confrontation, resolution. So does every great 30-second commercial.

buildup.text: Act 1 sets the world. Act 2 introduces conflict. Act 3 resolves it. Aristotle defined this 2,300 years ago.

discovery.text: Nike's 'Find Your Greatness' follows it exactly: ordinary people (setup), facing limits (conflict), pushing through.

twist.text: The three-act structure works in six-second ads too. Vine stars mastered setup-punchline in seconds.

climax.text: Whether it's a 60-second Super Bowl ad or a Facebook post, three acts give the audience a complete experience.

punchline.text: Setup, conflict, resolution. 2,300 years and it still works.

quiz.question: Who originally defined the three-act structure?

details.summary: The three-act structure — setup, confrontation, resolution — is storytelling's most foundational framework. In advertising, Act 1 establishes the customer's world and problem, Act 2 introduces the product as the solution amid challenges, and Act 3 delivers the satisfying transformation.
details.whyItMatters: Three-act structure gives any ad a beginning, middle, and end that feels complete and satisfying. It's the simplest working template for turning product information into an engaging narrative.
takeaways: Act 1 establishes character and problem to create audience identification
Act 2 raises stakes and introduces the brand as the turning point
Act 3 delivers resolution that makes the audience feel the product's value

faq.question: How long does each act need to be?
faq.answer: In a 30-second ad, Act 1 might be 8 seconds, Act 2 might be 15 seconds, and Act 3 might be 7 seconds. The proportions matter more than the durations — setup should be quick enough to maintain interest but thorough enough to create identification.

faq.question: Can the three-act structure work for static ads?
faq.answer: Yes. A print ad or social media image can imply all three acts in a single frame. Before/after images compress the entire arc into one visual. A headline can reference the problem (Act 1), the image shows the solution (Act 2), and the tagline delivers the resolution (Act 3).
